U1-S1-WTC-1 | WTC | U1-S1-IC3 | DOK 3 | 3E AUDITED
I can use evidence from a short scenario to decide whether a physics explanation is supported and explain why formulas in physics are guides for thinking, not just tools for calculation.
A class tests whether changing the release height of a toy car changes the distance it rolls after leaving a ramp. Use the shared data to break down the investigation. (a) List two quantities that were directly measured. (b) State one inference the data support. (c) Identify one variable that should be controlled in a repeat test. (d) Explain whether the claim “greater release height causes greater roll distance” is testable with this setup and what pattern would support it.
Release height (cm)Roll distance (cm)
542
1071
1596
20124
Teacher answer / alignment

Answer: (a) Release height and roll distance were measured. (b) The car generally rolled farther from greater release heights. (c) Acceptable controls include the same car, ramp, floor surface, and release method. (d) Yes. The claim is testable because both quantities are measurable; a consistent increase in roll distance as release height increases would support it.

Evidence job: navigate a multipart evidence/model task: identify what is observed, interpret the shared data/model, plan an evidence test, and justify which conclusion is supported

Structure: WTC-FRQ-PREVIEW-01 | Family: U1-S1-wtc-frq-navigation

U1-S2-WTC-1 | WTC | U1-S2-IC3 | DOK 3 | 3E AUDITED
I can distinguish between “no forces acting” and “no net force acting.” and identify support force, weight, and other common forces in simple situations.
A cart moves to the right at constant speed while two horizontal forces act on it. Use the diagram to unpack the situation. (a) Identify what the equal arrow lengths tell you. (b) State the net horizontal force. (c) Predict the cart’s motion one second later if the forces stay the same. (d) Explain which part of Newton’s First Law supports your prediction.
Teacher answer / alignment

Answer: (a) The horizontal forces have equal magnitude and opposite direction. (b) The net horizontal force is 0 N. (c) The cart continues to the right at the same speed. (d) With zero net force, an object already moving maintains constant velocity.

Evidence job: navigate a multipart force/motion task: parse the chosen object, read a shared force diagram, identify dependencies, plan the force reasoning, and justify the motion conclusion

Structure: WTC-FRQ-PREVIEW-01 | Family: U1-S2-wtc-frq-navigation

U1-S3-WTC-1 | WTC | U1-S3-IC3 | DOK 3 | 3E AUDITED
I can identify the resultant force from a simple vector diagram and use arrow length and direction to compare force strength and direction.
Two students pull a wheeled crate in opposite directions. Use the shared vector model. (a) Before calculating, predict the direction of the resultant. (b) Determine the net force. (c) A third student wants the net force to become 0 N without changing the 14 N pull. What magnitude and direction should the other side have? (d) Explain why direction must be included when combining the forces.
Teacher answer / alignment

Answer: (a) Right, because 14 N right is larger than 9 N left. (b) 5 N right. (c) 14 N left. (d) Forces are vectors; opposite directions subtract rather than simply adding magnitudes.

Evidence job: navigate a multipart vector task: interpret scaled arrows, plan a resultant method, carry a short analysis, and justify a comparison from the shared vector model

Structure: WTC-FRQ-PREVIEW-01 | Family: U1-S3-wtc-frq-navigation

U1-S4-WTC-1 | WTC | U1-S4-IC3 | DOK 3 | 3E AUDITED
I can explain why an object moving at constant speed in a straight line can be in equilibrium and use the equilibrium rule to reason about upward/downward and left/right forces.
A stage light hangs motionless from a vertical cable. Use the force model. (a) Identify the evidence that the light is in static equilibrium. (b) Determine the missing upward force if the light’s weight is 120 N. (c) Predict what would happen immediately if the upward force dropped to 100 N while weight stayed 120 N. (d) Explain how the equilibrium rule connects the force model to the motion prediction.
Evidence / forceValue
Motionat rest
Upward cable force?
Weight120 N downward
Teacher answer / alignment

Answer: (a) It is motionless and the forces are balanced. (b) 120 N upward. (c) The net force becomes 20 N downward, so its velocity begins changing downward. (d) Equilibrium requires ΣF=0; once the forces no longer sum to zero, the object accelerates in the net-force direction.

Evidence job: navigate a multipart equilibrium task: extract givens from a shared model, identify a balance relationship, analyze a missing force, and justify the motion state

Structure: WTC-FRQ-PREVIEW-01 | Family: U1-S4-wtc-frq-navigation

U1-S5-WTC-1 | WTC | U1-S5-IC3 | DOK 3 | 3E AUDITED
I can explain how the net force affects the object’s motion and critique an incorrect force explanation and revise it using physics vocabulary.
A student models a book resting on a table with the diagram below. The student claims, “The downward arrow is the force the book exerts on the table, so the two arrows cancel on the book.” (a) Define the system being modeled. (b) Identify what is wrong with the student’s explanation. (c) Revise the force labels so the model contains only forces acting on the book. (d) Use the revised model to explain why the book can remain at rest.
Teacher answer / alignment

Answer: (a) The system is the book. (b) A force the book exerts on the table acts on the table, not on the book. (c) The forces on the book are its weight downward and the table’s support force upward. (d) Those two forces can be equal and opposite, giving zero net force, so the book remains at rest.

Evidence job: navigate a multipart model-critique task: identify the system, inspect a shared flawed model/evidence set, plan a revision, and defend the revised motion explanation

Structure: WTC-FRQ-PREVIEW-01 | Family: U1-S5-wtc-frq-navigation

U1-S1-EXIT-A-Q1 | Exit_Ticket | U1-S1-IC1 | DOK 2 | 3E AUDITED
I can distinguish between an observation, inference, hypothesis, law, and theory.
A photogate records that a cart takes 1.42 s to cross a marked interval. A student says, “The rough patch on the track slowed the cart.” Classify the recorded time and the student statement as observation or inference.
Teacher answer / alignment

Answer: The 1.42 s time is an observation/measurement. The claim about the rough patch is an inference because it explains the measurement.

Evidence job: core classification of observation/inference/scientific knowledge category

U1-S1-EXIT-A-Q2 | Exit_Ticket | U1-S1-IC2 | DOK 2 | 3E AUDITED
I can explain why a claim must be testable to be scientific.
A student claims, “This flashlight has a stronger beam because it looks more powerful.” Explain why the claim is not testable as written, then give one measurable revision.
Teacher answer / alignment

Answer: “Looks more powerful” is not a defined measurement. A testable revision could compare light-meter readings from the two flashlights at the same distance under the same room conditions.

TripDistance (m)Time (s)

263
362

I can explain that inertia is a property of matter, not a force.
Which statement about a tool chest and other matter uses the idea of inertia correctly?

  2. An object at rest has no inertia.
  3. More massive objects have more inertia, a property that resists changes in motion.

Teacher answer / alignment

Answer: Inertia is a property of matter associated with resistance to changes in motion; it is not a force and exists whether the object is moving or at rest.

U1-SUM-V6-Q02 | Summative V6 | U1-S4-IC1 | DOK 2 | 3E AUDITED
I can recognize static equilibrium and dynamic equilibrium.
Consider three cases: I. a book rests on a shelf; II. an elevator moves upward at constant velocity; III. a car travels around a circular exit ramp at constant speed. Which classification is correct?
  1. I and II are equilibrium cases; III is not
  2. Only I is equilibrium
  3. All three are dynamic equilibrium
  4. II and III are equilibrium because both are moving
Teacher answer / alignment

Answer: Static equilibrium is rest with zero net force; dynamic equilibrium is constant straight-line velocity with zero net force. Direction-changing motion requires acceleration and therefore a nonzero net force.
